description: The four core perspectives — functionalism, Marxism, feminism and interactionism — and their key claims.
content_html:
Why Perspectives Matter

A sociological perspective is a theoretical lens through which sociologists interpret the social world. No single perspective commands universal agreement; instead, sociology is a discipline of competing theoretical frameworks, each illuminating different aspects of society. GCSE Sociology requires you to know, compare and apply four core perspectives — functionalism, Marxism, feminism and interactionism — across every topic you study.

A key skill in sociology is being able to state what each perspective argues, who the named sociologists are, and how each perspective differs from the others. In your extended responses, naming the perspective before making a claim is essential: “From a Marxist perspective…” or “Feminists argue that…” signals that you are operating at the level of sociological analysis rather than personal opinion.

Functionalism: Society as a Working System

Functionalism is a consensus perspective. Functionalists argue that society resembles a biological organism: each institution (the family, education, religion, the economy) performs necessary functions that contribute to the survival and stability of the whole. Society is held together by value consensus — a shared agreement on core values.

Durkheim is the founding functionalist thinker. Parsons extended this framework to argue that the family performs two irreplaceable functions: the primary socialisation of children and the stabilisation of adult personalities. For functionalists, social inequality, where it exists, can serve a functional purpose: Davis and Moore argued that higher rewards for more demanding roles act as incentives for talented individuals to train for them, ensuring important positions are filled effectively.

Critics argue that functionalism is politically conservative: it tends to justify existing arrangements as functional and necessary, making it difficult to explain persistent inequality as anything other than a natural sorting mechanism. Marxists and feminists argue that functionalism ignores the role of power and conflict in shaping institutions that ostensibly serve “society” but in practice serve dominant groups.

Key Fact

Functionalism is a consensus perspective: shared norms and values hold society together and institutions serve everyone’s interests. Marxism and feminism are conflict perspectives: society is divided by class exploitation (Marxism) or patriarchy (feminism). Both are macro perspectives, explaining behaviour through large-scale structures. Interactionism is a micro perspective, focusing on face-to-face interactions and meanings.

Marxism: Society as Class Conflict

Marxism is a conflict perspective. Marxists argue that capitalist society is fundamentally divided between the bourgeoisie (who own the means of production) and the proletariat (who must sell their labour). All major social institutions — the family, education, the law, religion — serve to reproduce and legitimate this exploitative relationship. The ruling class maintains control not only through economic power but through ideological control: promoting ideas via the media, religion and education that make the existing order appear natural and just.

Marx argued that the dominant ideas of any age are the ideas of the dominant class. Workers are kept in a state of false consciousness, accepting their own subordination as inevitable. Bowles and Gintis later applied this framework to education, arguing that schools reproduce the workforce capitalism needs through the correspondence principle — matching attitudes and behaviours in school (obedience, punctuality, deference to authority) to those required in the workplace.

Functionalism: society is based on consensus; institutions perform functions for the benefit of society as a whole; inequality reflects functional necessity. Key thinkers: Durkheim, Parsons, Davis and Moore.

Marxism: society is based on class conflict; institutions serve the interests of the ruling class; inequality is the product of exploitation, not merit. Key thinkers: Marx, Bowles and Gintis.

Both are macro (structural) perspectives: they explain individual behaviour by reference to large-scale social structures. They differ fundamentally on whether those structures are consensual or coercive.

Feminism: Society as Patriarchal

Feminism is a conflict perspective that focuses on gender inequality. Feminists argue that society is patriarchal — structured so that men hold structural power and women are systematically disadvantaged. Walby identified six structures of patriarchy: paid employment, household production, culture, sexuality, violence and the state. Together these operate across public and private life to maintain male dominance.

Feminism is not a single perspective but a family of related arguments. Liberal feminism argues that legal reforms and changing attitudes can achieve gender equality. Marxist feminism argues that women’s oppression is tied to capitalism: women provide unpaid domestic labour that sustains the workforce, benefiting the capitalist class. Radical feminism argues that patriarchy is an autonomous system of male domination that cannot be dismantled simply by legal or economic reform; it requires a fundamental reorganisation of social relations between men and women.

Key Fact

Key thinkers by perspective: Functionalism — Durkheim (boundary maintenance), Parsons (primary socialisation); Marxism — Bowles and Gintis (correspondence principle), Marx (false consciousness); Feminism — Walby (six structures of patriarchy); Interactionism — Becker (labelling, master status).

Interactionism: Society as Meaning-Making

Interactionism focuses on the small-scale, everyday interactions through which individuals construct and negotiate meaning. Rather than starting with large-scale structures, interactionists ask: what does this situation mean to the people in it? How do labels applied by powerful actors shape individuals’ self-concepts and behaviour?

Becker’s labelling theory (Outsiders, 1963) is the key interactionist contribution to crime and deviance. Becker argued that deviance is not an inherent quality of an act but a label applied by those with the power to define and enforce rules. A master status — such as “criminal” or “failure” — can come to override all other aspects of a person’s identity. If a student is labelled as a troublemaker, teachers may interpret all their behaviour through that lens, and the student may eventually internalise the label, producing a self-fulfilling prophecy.

The New Right: A Fifth Perspective

In addition to the four core perspectives, the New Right perspective appears throughout the GCSE Sociology specification, particularly in relation to the family, poverty and crime. New Right thinkers argue that the welfare state has created a dependency culture — a cycle in which individuals and families come to rely on state benefits rather than developing self-reliance and personal responsibility. Murray argued that an underclass has emerged in Britain and the United States, characterised by welfare dependency, family breakdown and high rates of crime, and that this is caused not by structural poverty but by perverse welfare incentives that remove motivation to work. Critics of the New Right — particularly Marxists and feminists — argue that Murray’s analysis blames the poor for structural inequalities produced by the capitalist economy and that it ignores the gender implications of policies that push women back into financial dependence.

Students often conflate interactionism with the other three perspectives. A clear distinction: functionalism, Marxism and feminism are all structural (macro) perspectives — they explain individual behaviour by reference to large-scale forces (value consensus, class, patriarchy). Interactionism is a micro perspective — it starts from the individual interaction and the meanings people construct. Both levels of analysis are valid: structural perspectives explain patterns (why working-class students underachieve on average); interactionist perspectives explain processes (how specific labels applied by specific teachers contribute to that pattern in practice).
exam_tip_html: The 12-mark Evaluate question will often invite you to compare perspectives. The most common error is to describe all four perspectives without evaluating them — this caps you in the Developing tier. To reach Secure or Mastering, you must: compare (“Unlike functionalists, who argue…, Marxists contend…”), evaluate (“A limitation of the functionalist view is that it ignores…”), and judge (“On balance, the feminist perspective is more convincing because…”). Never describe all four perspectives as equally valid without explaining why you find one more or less convincing than another. The examiner is looking for a reasoned judgement, not a balanced description.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Functionalism (consensus, macro) argues society is held together by shared values and institutions perform necessary functions. Marxism (conflict, macro) argues society is divided by class exploitation and institutions serve the ruling class.
  • Feminism (conflict, macro) argues society is patriarchal — three strands: liberal (legal reform), Marxist (capitalism + gender), radical (patriarchy as autonomous system, e.g. Walby’s six structures).
  • Interactionism (micro) focuses on face-to-face interaction, labelling and meaning. Becker’s master status (1963) shows how labels can produce a self-fulfilling prophecy. The New Right (Murray) argues welfare dependency creates an underclass — challenged by Marxist and feminist critics.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociological perspective argues that society is held together by value consensus and that social institutions perform necessary functions for the benefit of all?
A) Marxism
B) Feminism
C) Functionalism
D) Interactionism
Define the term 'patriarchy' as used by sociologists.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying patriarchy as a system involving male power or dominance; 1 mark for indicating it is structural and systematically disadvantages women in both public and private life. Example: 'Patriarchy is a social system in which men hold structural power over women, disadvantaging women across public spheres such as work and politics, and private spheres such as the family.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one feature of the interactionist perspective and describe how it differs from a structural perspective such as Marxism.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying an interactionist feature (e.g. focus on micro-level interactions, labelling, master status, self-fulfilling prophecy, subjective meaning). Up to 2 marks for a developed description of how it differs. Example: identifying Becker's concept of labelling (1 mark) and explaining that where Marxists explain educational underachievement by reference to the large-scale class structure and the correspondence principle (Bowles and Gintis), interactionists focus on how specific labels applied by individual teachers generate a self-fulfilling prophecy, explaining the same outcome through face-to-face processes rather than structural forces (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe the key ideas of the Marxist perspective on how society works.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for describing class structure: society is divided between the bourgeoisie (who own the means of production) and the proletariat (who must sell their labour); the bourgeoisie exploit the proletariat by taking profit from workers' labour. Up to 2 marks for ideological control or false consciousness: the ruling class maintains dominance not only through economic power but by promoting ideas through education, media and religion that make exploitation appear natural; false consciousness prevents the working class from recognising their own position. Credit for naming Bowles and Gintis and the correspondence principle.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that the Marxist perspective gives the most convincing account of how social institutions work.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments in favour: Marxists show how institutions (education, family, media) reproduce class inequality; Bowles and Gintis demonstrate the correspondence between school hierarchies and workplace hierarchies; evidence of persistent class-based attainment gaps supports structural analysis. Arguments against: functionalists argue institutions serve all of society, not just the ruling class; Davis and Moore's meritocracy model suggests inequality is functional; interactionists argue Marxism ignores individual agency and the role of labelling; feminists argue Marxism underplays gender as a structural force. The answer names at least two contrasting perspectives with named sociologists, uses sociological vocabulary, and reaches a clear supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides addressed; at least one named contrasting perspective; a judgement reached.

Developing: Mostly descriptive of Marxism; some criticism noted but undeveloped; conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic description of Marxism; little comparison; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that the functionalist perspective is too conservative to explain the inequalities found in modern British society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of arguments for both sides. Arguments that functionalism is too conservative: it justifies inequality as functional (Davis and Moore) rather than exposing it as exploitative; Marxists (Bowles and Gintis) show institutions serve the ruling class, not society as a whole; feminists (Walby) show patriarchal structures are maintained by institutions functionalism treats as neutral; evidence of structural inequalities by class, gender and ethnicity challenges the notion of value consensus. Arguments that functionalism retains explanatory value: it explains social order and why most people most of the time follow norms; Parsons' analysis of primary socialisation explains cultural transmission; functionalists accept inequality exists and argue it performs a motivational function (Davis and Moore). The answer compares at least two named perspectives, uses key vocabulary (value consensus, false consciousness, patriarchy, correspondence principle), weighs both sides, and arrives at a clear supported conclusion.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present; both sides covered; named sociologists referenced; a clear judgement reached.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided; some named theorists; conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic description; few named sociologists; no clear judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which perspective focuses on face-to-face interactions and the labels attached to individuals by powerful actors?
Walby's six structures of patriarchy belong to which sociological perspective?
Functionalists argue that society is held together by a '______ consensus' — shared agreement on core norms and values.
Becker's concept of '______ status' describes how a single label (such as 'criminal') can come to dominate all other aspects of a person's identity.
Match each perspective to its key claim about society.
right: Society is held together by shared values; institutions perform necessary functions
Society is divided by class conflict; institutions serve the ruling class
Society is patriarchal; institutions maintain male power over women
Social behaviour is shaped by labelling and the meanings individuals construct in interaction

flashcard_questions.a: Functionalist concept: the shared agreement on core norms and values that holds society together.
Each institution performs a necessary function contributing to the stability of society as a whole.
Institutions serve the interests of the bourgeoisie and reproduce class exploitation.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the correspondence principle (Bowles and Gintis)?
flashcard_questions.a: The argument that attitudes and hierarchies in school directly mirror those expected in capitalist workplaces.
A system in which men hold structural power and women are systematically disadvantaged in both public and private life.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two public-sphere structures of patriarchy identified by Walby.
flashcard_questions.a: Paid employment and the state: both disadvantage women in the labour market and in political power.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two private-sphere structures of patriarchy identified by Walby.
flashcard_questions.a: Household production and sexuality: Walby argues women perform unpaid domestic labour and face control of their sexuality.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the remaining two structures of patriarchy in Walby's framework?
flashcard_questions.a: Culture and violence: patriarchal norms are reproduced through cultural representations and reinforced by male violence.
A label (e.g. 'criminal') that overrides all other aspects of a person's social identity.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the self-fulfilling prophecy in interactionism?
flashcard_questions.a: When a person internalises a label and acts in ways that confirm it, making the original prediction come true.

flashcard_questions.q: Murray's New Right: what is the underclass?
flashcard_questions.a: A group characterised by welfare dependency, family breakdown and high crime rates, caused by perverse welfare incentives.

flashcard_questions.q: Difference between macro and micro perspectives?
flashcard_questions.a: Macro perspectives (functionalism, Marxism, feminism) explain behaviour through large-scale structures; micro (interactionism) focuses on face-to-face interactions.

flashcard_questions.q: Liberal feminism: how is gender equality achieved?
flashcard_questions.a: Through legal reforms and changing social attitudes rather than a fundamental reorganisation of society.

flashcard_questions.q: Radical feminism: cause of gender inequality?
flashcard_questions.a: Patriarchy as an autonomous system of male domination across all areas of social life.

glossary_terms.definition: A consensus perspective seeing society as a system of interrelated parts, each performing necessary functions to maintain stability through shared values.
The functionalist concept of broad agreement among members of society on core norms and values, enabling cooperation and social order.
A conflict perspective arguing that capitalist society is divided between bourgeoisie and proletariat, with institutions serving to reproduce class exploitation.
Bowles and Gintis's argument that attitudes, behaviours and hierarchies in schools directly mirror those required in capitalist workplaces.
A range of perspectives arguing that society is structured by patriarchy, systematically disadvantaging women in both public and private life.
A social system in which men hold structural power over women, operating across institutions such as the family, workplace and the state.
A micro-level perspective focusing on face-to-face interactions and the subjective meanings individuals construct, including the effects of labelling.
Becker's term for a label that overrides all other aspects of a person's identity and shapes how others interact with them.

hero_image_caption: Four competing perspectives — functionalism, Marxism, feminism and interactionism — form the theoretical core of GCSE Sociology.
